paper_summary: This paper introduces GRADINO, a from-scratch benchmark generator for numerical question answering over multiple non-relational tables. GRADINO synthesizes a latent relational source to derive executable SQL supervision and gold answers, then renders perturbed non-relational views (hierarchical pivots, merged headers, blank rows, typographical noise, unit conversions, OCR noise) that hide clean schemas while preserving answer verifiability via provenance masks. It supports two evidence-flow topologies: parallel (one scalar per table then aggregate) and sequential (lookup-key propagation across tables before aggregation). The system verbalizes SQL programs into natural-language questions and runs an LLM-based verification/repair pass. Experiments in financial and environmental domains evaluate several LLMs (gpt-5-mini and Qwen family) across varying table counts (up to 20 for parallel), aggregation types, and unit settings. Main findings: (1) model accuracy collapses as the number of non-relational tables increases; (2) sequential chains are harder per table than parallel aggregation; (3) unit heterogeneity induces large, domain-dependent performance drops; (4) GRADINO-generated data can meaningfully augment scarce in-domain multi-table supervision. The authors provide manual verification statistics, ablations on real tables, prompt templates, and a discussion of limitations and ethics, and they release code and generated datasets.
summary_of_strengths: 1) Novel, well-motivated generator: GRADINO is a principled from-scratch framework that decouples supervision (executable SQL over a latent relational source) from presentation (perturbed non-relational views), enabling controlled experiments that prior datasets cannot easily support. 2) Clear taxonomy and generation of multi-table topologies: explicit parallel and sequential evidence-flow patterns allow targeted stress tests of model capabilities. 3) Strong empirical findings: systematic experiments show a striking multi-table non-relational blind spot in contemporary LLMs, including scaling behavior and unit-heterogeneity effects, validated both on synthetic and perturbed real tables. 4) Practical utility: GRADINO-generated data improves finetuning performance and complements scarce in-domain supervision (e.g., GRI-QA). 5) Careful methodology: SQL supervision ensures verifiable answers, solver-backed semantic constraints increase plausibility, and manual verification shows high question fidelity. 6) Reproducibility support: the paper provides prompts, methodological detail, and states that code/datasets will be released.
summary_of_weaknesses: 1) Realism trade-off: GRADINO intentionally sacrifices some real-world visual/semantic realism for controllability; certain visual cues (alignment, charts, highly irregular spreadsheets) and document-specific artifacts are not modeled, so findings may not fully generalize to all production settings. 2) Narrow task scope: the focus is on numerical scalar aggregation questions; other important multi-table reasoning types (e.g., set operations, textual reasoning across tables, logical aggregations) are not covered. 3) Generator-model coupling: parts of the generation and verification pipeline rely on an internal LLM (gpt-5-mini). Although the authors evaluate other models and inspect for bias, using the same LLM in generation and some evaluations raises the possibility of subtle generation-style artifacts or distributional bias. 4) Question verbalization errors: sequential question verbalization is more error-prone (∼7.5% error observed); the repair step depends on LLMs and could be strengthened by additional human validation. 5) Evaluation breadth: experiments use a limited set of model families (gpt-5-mini and Qwen variants); including a larger variety of LLMs and specialized table models (or non-LLM baselines) would give a fuller picture of robustness.
comments_suggestions_typos: Suggested improvements: (a) add more illustrative failure-case examples (tables + model reasoning traces) in the appendix so readers can see concrete error patterns; (b) include a small human-judged realism evaluation of generated tables (domain experts rate realism) to complement the solver-based plausibility checks; (c) ablate supervision targets for finetuning (final answer only vs full reasoning trace) to quantify the contribution of trace supervision; (d) expand model diversity in experiments if possible, and, in the repository, publish generation seeds and configuration files to ease reproduction. Minor: a short explicit paragraph in the main text addressing potential generator-overfitting (why gpt-5-mini-as-generator does not advantage gpt-5-mini-as-evaluator) would preempt reader concerns.
limitations_and_societal_impact: The authors explicitly discuss limitations (synthetic realism, restricted numerical focus, question verbalization errors) and ethical considerations (no PII, use of public datasets for validation). Remaining discussion items: potential bias introduced by LLM-generated lexical choices and unit conventions (regional or domain-specific vocabulary), and the risk that strong benchmark performance on synthetic diagnostic data be misread as production readiness. The paper positions GRADINO as a diagnostic tool, which mitigates misuse, but a brief expansion on lexicon/regional coverage and recommended usage guidelines for practitioners would strengthen the impact section.
ethical_concerns: No major ethical concerns. The dataset is synthetic (fictional entities), public crawled tables used for validation are public and used only for testing, and the authors discuss privacy and ethical considerations. The paper does not appear to violate ACL Code of Ethics.
